label: Linear Inequalities in Two Variables
overview: A linear inequality in two variables defines a half-plane on the coordinate plane. SAT questions ask you to identify the correct shaded region for a given inequality, determine whether a point satisfies the inequality, or match a real-world constraint to its graph. The boundary line is dashed for strict inequalities and solid for non-strict.

keyFormulas.name: Test a point
keyFormulas.latex: \text{Substitute point into inequality; if true, shade that side}

keyFormulas.name: Rearranged form
keyFormulas.latex: y > mx + b \Rightarrow \text{shade above}; \quad y < mx + b \Rightarrow \text{shade below}

workedExamples.problem: Which of the following points satisfies the inequality 3x − 2y < 6? (A) (4, 0)  (B) (0, −4)  (C) (1, 0)  (D) (2, 3)

commonMistakes.mistake: Shading below the line when the inequality says y > (and vice versa)
commonMistakes.fix: y > (mx + b) means y-values are greater than the line, so shade above. y < means shade below.

commonMistakes.mistake: Drawing a solid boundary for a strict inequality
commonMistakes.fix: Strict < or > use a dashed boundary (points on the line are NOT solutions). Non-strict ≤ or ≥ use a solid line.

quickTip: After drawing the boundary, test the point (0, 0) in the inequality. If it satisfies it, shade the side containing (0, 0); otherwise shade the other side.
